Reliability coefficients for a Rasch model

Source: R/reliability.R
RMreliability.Rd

Computes four reliability coefficients for a Rasch or partial credit model: Cronbach's alpha, the person separation index (PSI, the WLE-based separation reliability), the marginal reliability (the mean of the conditional reliability curve over the estimated latent distribution), and the relative measurement uncertainty (RMU, RMUreliability()) from plausible values drawn with mirt::fscores().

Usage

RMreliability(
  data,
  conf_int = 0.95,
  draws = 1000,
  rmu_iter = 50,
  estim = "WLE",
  boot = FALSE,
  boot_iter = 200,
  parallel = TRUE,
  n_cores = NULL,
  seed = NULL,
  verbose = FALSE,
  theta_range = c(-10, 10),
  output = "kable"
)

Arguments

data

A data.frame or matrix of item responses, items scored from 0. See Details for how missing values are handled.

conf_int

Numeric in (0, 1). HDCI width of the bootstrap intervals and of RMU. Default 0.95.

draws

Integer. Number of plausible values drawn from the mirt model for RMU. Default 1000. More draws give a more stable RMU, at a cost that grows about linearly.

rmu_iter

Integer. How many times RMUreliability() is repeated on the same draws, each with a new random split of the columns. The estimates are averaged over the repetitions. Default 50.

estim

Character. Estimator used by mirt::fscores() as the starting point for the plausible values: "WLE" (default), "EAP", "MAP" or "ML". The plausible values themselves are drawn by Metropolis-Hastings. PSI and the marginal reliability do not use it.

boot

Logical. Bootstrap confidence intervals for alpha, PSI and the marginal reliability. Default FALSE.

boot_iter

Integer. Number of bootstrap samples with boot = TRUE. Default 200.

parallel

Logical. Run the bootstrap in parallel via mirai when it is installed. Default TRUE.

n_cores

Integer or NULL. Number of parallel workers. When NULL, getOption("mc.cores") is used. If that is unset too, the bootstrap runs sequentially.

seed

Integer or NULL. Random seed for reproducibility. See easyRasch2-reproducibility for what this guarantees and how it interacts with parallel.

verbose

Logical. Print progress messages and a progress bar for the bootstrap. Default FALSE.

theta_range

Numeric vector of length 2. Theta limits passed to mirt::fscores(). Default c(-10, 10).

output

Character. "kable" (default) for a knitr::kable() table, or "dataframe".

Value

  • output = "kable": a knitr_kable table with one row per coefficient.

  • output = "dataframe": a data.frame with the columns metric ("Cronbach's alpha", "PSI", "Marginal (curve mean)" and "RMU (<estim>)"), estimate, lower, upper and notes.

Details

With boot = TRUE, alpha, PSI and the marginal reliability get confidence intervals from a nonparametric bootstrap that resamples respondents and recomputes the coefficients without refitting a mirt model. The RMU interval is the HDCI of the correlations across plausible-value draws, averaged over rmu_iter random splits of the draws.

Data. Respondents with no responses are dropped. Cronbach's alpha uses complete cases. PSI and the marginal reliability use every respondent's answered items, and PSI leaves out respondents with the lowest or highest possible score (see below). At least one complete case is needed.

Marginal reliability is the mean of the conditional reliability curve over the latent density, \(\int \sigma^2/(\sigma^2 + 1/I(\theta))\, g(\theta)\,d\theta\). The test information \(I(\theta)\) is summed from the CML item parameters, and \(g\) is the normal latent density \(N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with both parameters estimated by marginal maximum likelihood with the items fixed. Integrating over the estimated distribution, rather than the \(N(0,1)\) that mirt::marginal_rxx() assumes, keeps it correct on the Rasch logit scale, where \(\sigma\) is often well above 1 and an \(N(0,1)\) assumption underestimates reliability.

Up to version 1.3.0 \(\mu\) was held at 0. Centring the item thresholds fixes the item mean, not where the respondents are, so a normal density pinned to 0 could reach an off-target sample only by widening. \(\sigma\) then absorbed the mistargeting, and marginal reliability rose as targeting got worse. See the note under Value in RMreliabilityCurve() for the size of the effect.

The marginal reliability is the model-based counterpart of the sample-based PSI. PSI divides by the observed spread of the WLE estimates, the marginal reliability uses the fitted latent density. A large gap between them flags an off-target or non-normal sample, and since version 1.3.1 both fall when targeting gets worse.

How it relates to published coefficients. The reported value is none of the coefficients named in the literature.

It is the mean of a curve, not a ratio of averages. The classical latent-scale reliability is one variance ratio, \(\sigma^2/(\sigma^2 + \overline{SEM^2})\) (Milanzi et al., 2015, section 3.2, with a constant error variance). Here the ratio is averaged over the latent density instead. Since \(\sigma^2/(\sigma^2 + x)\) is convex in \(x\), the mean of the curve is the larger of the two (Jensen's inequality). The choice was made on accuracy: averaging the curve tracked the exact expected-sum-score reliability more closely than the ratio of averages in an internal replication (mean absolute error 0.015 against 0.018 for binary data, 0.010 against 0.015 for polytomous).

It is a latent-scale quantity checked against a manifest criterion. Milanzi et al. (2015) argue that interest usually lies in the reliability of observed scores, and that latent coefficients run consistently higher. This one was therefore validated against the exact expected-sum-score reliability, \(Var(\mu)/(Var(\mu) + Var(\epsilon))\), and tracked it to within about 0.02 in the conditions tested. It remains a latent-scale coefficient that approximates a manifest one.

Milanzi et al. recommend something this package does not implement. They favour Taylor-series manifest reliability measures, which approximate \(Var(\mu)\) and \(Var(\epsilon)\) on the observed-score scale directly. In the same internal replication those were the most accurate (0.012). They are cited here for their criticism of the subtractive coefficient, which this package acted on, not for their remedy.

Up to version 1.2.0 this row used the subtractive coefficient \(1 - \overline{1/I(\theta)}/\sigma^2\) (Green et al., 1984, Milanzi et al.'s equation 12, attributed there to Lord, 1980). It can fall below zero when the average error variance exceeds the trait variance, and much of the gap between PSI and that coefficient came from the different formulas rather than the sample. It is still returned as the marginal_green attribute of RMreliabilityCurve() for comparison.

PSI is the WLE-based separation reliability, \(1 - \overline{SEM^2} / \mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta)\), from the CML item thresholds (psychotools) and the WLE person locations and their SEMs. Respondents with the lowest or highest possible raw score are left out, since their boundary estimates would inflate the person variance and overstate reliability. Earlier versions used eRm::SepRel() with MLE, and the values can differ, most for scales with many extreme scores, such as dichotomous items.

RMU follows Bignardi, Kievit and Bürkner (2026), here with plausible values from mirt rather than fully Bayesian posterior draws (see Mislevy, 1991, for plausible values).

Bootstrap samples that cannot be fitted are dropped, with a message giving how many and why. The usual reason is a sparse lowest or middle response category that is missing from the sample.

References

Bignardi, G., Kievit, R., & Bürkner, P. C. (2026). A general method for estimating reliability using Bayesian Measurement Uncertainty. PsyArXiv. https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/h54k8

Green, B. F., Bock, R. D., Humphreys, L. G., Linn, R. L., & Reckase, M. D. (1984). Technical Guidelines for Assessing Computerized Adaptive Tests. Journal of Educational Measurement, 21(4), 347–360. doi:10.1111/j.1745-3984.1984.tb01039.x

Milanzi, E., Molenberghs, G., Alonso, A., Verbeke, G., & De Boeck, P. (2015). Reliability measures in item response theory: Manifest versus latent correlation functions. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 68(1), 43-64. doi:10.1111/bmsp.12033

Mislevy, R. J. (1991). Randomization-Based Inference about Latent Variables from Complex Samples. Psychometrika, 56(2), 177-196. doi:10.1007/BF02294457

See also

RMreliabilityCurve() for precision along the scale, RMUreliability(), RMpersonParameters().

Examples

# \donttest{
if (requireNamespace("ggdist", quietly = TRUE) &&
    requireNamespace("eRm", quietly = TRUE)) {
  set.seed(1)
  RMreliability(eRm::raschdat1[, 1:20], draws = 1000)

  # Bootstrap intervals for alpha, PSI and the marginal reliability
  # (use 200 or more bootstrap samples in real analyses)
  RMreliability(eRm::raschdat1[, 1:20], draws = 1000,
                boot = TRUE, boot_iter = 25, parallel = FALSE, seed = 42)
}
#> 
#> 
#> Table: Reliability for 20 items, n = 100 respondents. PSI is the WLE-based separation reliability and excludes min/max scoring respondents. Marginal is the latent-density-weighted mean of the conditional reliability curve, sigma^2 / (sigma^2 + SEM(theta)^2).
#> 
#> |Metric                | Estimate| Lower (95% HDCI)| Upper (95% HDCI)|Notes                       |
#> |:---------------------|--------:|----------------:|----------------:|:---------------------------|
#> |Cronbach's alpha      |    0.754|            0.701|            0.813|25 bootstrap resamples      |
#> |PSI                   |    0.725|            0.673|            0.768|25 bootstrap resamples      |
#> |Marginal (curve mean) |    0.748|            0.699|            0.798|25 bootstrap resamples      |
#> |RMU (WLE)             |    0.753|            0.684|            0.817|1000 PVs, 50 RMU iterations |
# }
